newsitem.title: USA: Brazil debt may weather bribe scandal -US analysts.
newsitem.headline: Brazil debt may weather bribe scandal -US analysts.

text.p: Allegations of bribery in the Brazilian government should not sour investors' outlook for the country's debt unless they hamper privatization efforts or block the reelection amendment, U.S. analysts said Wednesday.
Analysts have held onto a neutral to slightly negative recommendation for Brazil debt, with most suggesting a wait-and-see approach to the developing scandal news.
Brazilian newspaper Folha de Sao Paolo alleged Tuesday that governors of the states of Acre and Amazonas paid five deputies to vote favorably on a reelection amendment.
On Wednesday, the paper said taped telephone conversations implicated Communications Minister Sergio Motta in the scheme.
Dan Peirce, chief emerging markets strategist at Bank of Boston, recommended lightening overweight Brazil positions but said investors who are underweight might see a buying opportunity.
"This is the first opportunity you've had to buy Brazil at a significant discount to Argentina in a long time," he said.
In early afternoon trading, Brazil "C" bonds BR8D14=RR were off 1/2 at 75-1/2 bid.

When the first scandal reports surfaced Tuesday, analysts intially said the scandal should blow over without hurting President Henrique Cardoso or his administration's reforms. On Wednesday, analysts said the alleged link to Motta raised new concerns.

"If there's proof that Motta is implicated, it will be more difficult for the Cardoso administration because he is a member of the cabinet. But there doesn't seem to be any proof yet," said William Romary, senior economist for Latin America at UBS Securities.

A committee of the Brazilian Senate was expected to decide Wednesday whether to introduce a constitutional amendment allowing presidents, state governors and mayors to run for a second consecutive term.
Many analysts saw the reelection of Cardoso as key to continuing economic reforms within the country.
"The reelection amendment is a pretty critical element," said Desmond Lachman, global emerging markets strategist at Salomon Brothers. "That heralds the way for real structural reform later on."
The cash-for-votes allegations remain fully unproven and do not appear to threaten Cardoso's reelection chances, Lachman said.
"Certainly this is having an impact on the market, but one doesn't want to jump too quickly to conclusions that it's going to torpedo the reelection effort," he said.

But the scandal could prolong the debate over the amendment, Brazil experts agreed. Support for the initiative remains solid, but the government may lack the ability to speed the legislation through Congress, they said.
"We can expect there will be some further delays, not necessarily postponements, but the discussions could drag out longer," Romary said.
Some analysts said the bribery allegations could delay privatization efforts. In particular, Motta's alleged involvement may cloud the outlook for telecom-sector privatization, they said.
A lower house panel was scheduled to vote Wednesday on a bill outlining the process of auctioning the national Telebras system.
"These allegations make it difficult to proceed with the agenda, which they really need to get done," Pierce said.
